newsitem.title: LEBANON: PAN ARAB GAMES-LEBANON SEEKS SYMBOLIC IRAQI PRESENCE.
newsitem.headline: PAN ARAB GAMES-LEBANON SEEKS SYMBOLIC IRAQI PRESENCE.

text.p: Lebanon, facing pressure from Gulf Arab states to exclude Iraq from the Pan Arab Games, is seeking a symbolic Iraqi presence following a request from the Arab League, a Lebanese foreign ministry official said on Wednesday.

"After a phone call from Esmat Abdel-Meguid, the secretary-general of the Arab League, Foreign Minister Faris Bouez started diplomatic contacts with Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to get their approval for at least symbolic Iraqi participation in the games," the official who requested anonymity told Reuters.
Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and other oil-rich Gulf Arab states had threatened to boycott the games which open in Beirut on Saturday if Iraq participated.
A source close to the games on Tuesday told Reuters that Iraqi athletes would not be granted visas to Lebanon.
Lebanon has been heavily promoting the games on television and Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri has paid several visits to the stadium which will house the games to underscore their importance.
But the games have been tarnished by Arab political rivalries before the first event started.

An official Iraqi newspaper on Wednesday condemned Lebanon's decision to exclude its athletes from the Pan Arab Games, calling the move an unjust action that does not represent the will of the Arab people.

Al-Thawra, the newspaper of Iraq's ruling Baath party, said that even the United States, which led the 1991 Gulf War to liberate Kuwait from Iraqi occupation, had not prevented Iraqi athletes from taking part in the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.
Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have maintained a hawkish stand on Iraq since the Gulf War but other Gulf Arab states have softened their line.
Kuwait says Iraq still holds some 600 Kuwaitis captured in the Gulf War when its forces invaded Kuwait in 1990, a charge denied by the Baghdad government.
Iraq and Kuwait were among 20 countries due to take part in the two-week games.

Lebanon, which has close ties with Kuwait, severed diplomatic ties with Baghdad in 1994 after the murder of an Iraqi dissident in Beirut. Four Iraqi diplomats suspected of involvement in the slaying were held in jail for three years. One of them died in jail.

Kuwait and Saudi Arabia have contributed substantially to the $50 million cost of rebuilding the 50,000-seat Beirut stadium at which many of the games' events will be held. They have also contributed millions of dollars to Lebanon's reconstruction.
The stadium was destroyed in an Israeli air raid during the Jewish state's 1982 invasion of Lebanon.
